extracted.intended_audience: princes, rulers, statesmen, and students of statecraft
extracted.subtask_description: Practical, prescriptive guidance for acquiring, governing, and preserving principalities — advice directed to rulers on military, political, and fiscal measures needed to gain and keep power. Draws on historical examples and practical maxims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify principalities correctly
rubrics_metrics.description: All states and powers are either republics or principalities. Principalities are either hereditary or new; new principalities may be wholly new or annexed to an existing hereditary state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin by identifying the kind of principality you have (hereditary vs new, annexed vs wholly new) because the methods for acquiring and preserving them differ materially. This classification underpins subsequent policy choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain hereditary customs and avoid change
rubrics_metrics.description: Hereditary states are easier to hold because it suffices not to transgress the customs of one's ancestors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not alter longstanding laws, taxes, or customs of a hereditary principality; prudent handling of circumstances will usually suffice for a ruler of average powers to keep his state unless extraordinary force intervenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: When annexing similar-language territories, extinguish the former ruling family and preserve laws/taxes
rubrics_metrics.description: Those dominions added to an ancient state of the same country and language are easiest to hold if the family of the former prince is destroyed and their laws and taxes are left unchanged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extinguishing the prior ruling family removes a focal point for revolt; keeping laws and taxes avoids alienating the populace. Example: Brittany, Burgundy, Gascony, Normandy annexed to France.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reside in newly acquired territories when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: When states are acquired in a country differing in language, customs, or laws, the prince should go and reside there to make his position secure and durable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical presence allows early detection and remedy of disorders, prevents officials from pillaging, and gives subjects prompt recourse to the prince; absence lets troubles grow until incurable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer colonies to garrisons
rubrics_metrics.description: Send colonies to key places rather than maintaining large garrisons; colonies are cheaper, more faithful, injure fewer citizens, and the injured are poor and scattered and cannot hurt you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Garrisons are costly and provoke widespread hardship and hostility; colonies offend only a minority and create loyal local anchors. Use colonies as 'keys' to a new state whenever feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Either treat those you injure well or crush them outright
rubrics_metrics.description: Men ought either to be well treated or crushed, because lighter injuries permit revenge while very serious injuries remove the possibility of retaliation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you must punish or dispossess, make the injury decisive so enemies cannot regroup; if you spare them, ensure they have no motive or means to rise. Avoid half-measures that allow reprisals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foresee and treat troubles early
rubrics_metrics.description: Foresee troubles and deal with them at once; when evils are foreseen they can be quickly redressed, but if permitted to grow they become incurable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a preventive mindset — the Romans' practice of addressing early disturbances avoided larger wars later. Don't wait until a problem is visible to everyone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be the head and defender of weaker neighbours; weaken stronger ones
rubrics_metrics.description: A prince who holds a different country ought to make himself the head and defender of his less powerful neighbours and to weaken the more powerful among them, preventing any foreign power as strong as himself from gaining a foothold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a balance among local states so none become strong enough to invite a foreign patron; use friendly relations with minor powers and keep greater neighbours humbled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect enemies from those you injured and disappointed friends
rubrics_metrics.description: In acquiring a new principality you have enemies among those you injured in seizing it, and you cannot always keep the friends who put you there because you may not satisfy their expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate internal opposition from dispossessed elites and from those who helped you expecting rewards; secure the goodwill of locals or neutralize threats through settlement, coercion, or institution-building.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use your own arms and abilities rather than the arms of others or fortune
rubrics_metrics.description: Principalities acquired by one's own arms and ability are more secure than those acquired by the arms of others or by fortune.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relying on mercenaries, auxiliaries, or luck leaves a ruler vulnerable when those supports fail. Build and maintain personal military capability and the loyalty of troops raised or commanded by you.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mercenaries and auxiliaries; they are dangerous and useless
rubrics_metrics.description: Mercenaries and auxiliaries are dangerous and unreliable; they often prove cowardly or self-interested and ultimately harmful to the prince who depends on them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer native, loyal forces under the prince's control. If auxiliaries are used, be conscious they serve their own masters' interests and can be a liability in crisis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure the strength of your principality realistically
rubrics_metrics.description: The strength of all principalities ought to be measured so that the prince understands the resources, loyalties, and military capacities he can rely on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess military forces, economic base, popular goodwill, geography, and institutional attachments; do not be deceived by superficial appearances of security.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose bold action over excessive caution; Fortune favors the bold
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the bold rather than the cautious man that will win and hold Fortune (and women, by Machiavelli's analogy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calculated boldness often achieves advantages that cautious delay forfeits; however, boldness must be combined with prudence and preparation to avoid ruin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prudence is choosing the least dangerous course
rubrics_metrics.description: In politics there are no perfectly safe courses; prudence consists in choosing the least dangerous ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh options by relative risks and long-term consequences rather than by unattainable moral purity; prefer policies that minimize existential threats to the state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crimes may win an empire but not glory; necessary wars are just
rubrics_metrics.description: While crimes may win an empire they do not win glory; necessary wars are just and the arms of a nation are hallowed when it has no other resource but to fight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the instrumental value of harsh measures for survival but be aware of moral and reputational limits; distinguish necessary, defensible actions from gratuitous cruelty if you value lasting renown.
